item.title: First Chapter: 'What Are Journalists For?'
item.description: This book review discusses Jay Rosen's advocacy for public journalism, a movement aiming to transform journalism by prioritizing citizen input and engagement. The review highlights the debate surrounding public journalism, with supporters viewing it as a way to improve political discourse and critics dismissing it as a fad or overreach. The review also notes the movement's waning influence in recent years, despite its impact on some news organizations.

item.title: Public Journalism A Case for Public Scholarship
item.description: Jay Rosen argues for "public journalism," a movement reforming the American press. He critiques the existing disconnect between journalism practice and academic theory, advocating for collaborative, participatory approaches that prioritize civic engagement and a deliberative public sphere. Rosen highlights examples of newspapers implementing these new practices, emphasizing the need for journalists to actively support public life and engage in a mutually beneficial relationship with scholars.

item.title: I Am Not Optimistic But I Do Have Hope: The Future of Journalism in A Media Age
item.description: This 1993 lecture distinguishes between 'journalism' and 'The Media,' arguing that journalism's purpose is to foster a public, not merely an audience. Rosen critiques the prevailing view of news as merely 'part of our world' and challenges the notion of journalistic objectivity as espoused by Leonard Downie Jr. He contrasts two visions of American democracy—Hamilton's emphasis on private gain and Jefferson's focus on public participation—and asserts that journalism should align with the latter, advocating for a reinvention of journalism to prevent its absorption into the media industry.

item.title: The Impossible Press: American Journalism and the Decline of Public Life
item.description: Rosen's doctoral dissertation traces the history of the idea that the function of the press is to inform the public. It argues that the rise of the mass circulation newspaper, while creating a technical ability to reach everyone, actually undermined the conditions necessary for a "universal town meeting." Drawing heavily on Walter Lippmann and John Dewey, it suggests that the professionalization of journalism ("objectivity") was a retreat from the problem of creating a genuine public life in a complex society. It contrasts news as "symptom" vs. news as "symbol" and explores how the press creates a "pseudo-environment" of public opinion.
